The Red-necked phalarope (Phalaropus lobatus) exhibits a striking reversal of typical avian sex roles, with females being the larger and more aggressively courting sex. Their eggs hatch after an incubation period of 19 days [ab = 19 days] when maintained at a nest temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a duration that aligns closely with that of other small-bodied shorebirds. Upon hatching, the precocial chicks emerge at a wet weight of approximately 4.0 grams [Wwb = approximately 4.0 grams], an initial mass that reflects their advanced state of development and capacity for self-feeding within hours of emergence. This relatively low hatchling mass is typical of the Scolopacidae and necessitates a rapid period of exogenous feeding to fuel subsequent growth. The downy young are brooded intermittently by the male parent but begin pecking at small invertebrate prey almost immediately, demonstrating the species' adaptation to cold, nutrient-poor arctic and subarctic breeding grounds.

Adult females of this species attain a significantly larger ultimate wet weight than males, with maximum recorded values reaching 37.4 grams [Wwi = 37.4 grams]. Males, in contrast, exhibit a more modest asymptotic body mass of approximately 32.4 grams [Wwi = approximately 32.4 grams], a dimorphism that underpins the reversed sexual selection observed in this taxon. These mass values are derived from field studies of breeding populations in the high Arctic and are consistent across the species' Holarctic range. The larger female body size is believed to facilitate the production of a full clutch, as females must accumulate sufficient reserves prior to laying. Following egg deposition, the female typically departs, leaving the smaller male to assume all incubation and brooding duties. This pattern of size dimorphism has been documented in comparative analyses of phalaropes and is thought to be driven by intense female competition for access to the limited pool of attentive males.

Within the typical thermal regime of active metabolism for this species, maintained at 41 °C [T = 41 °C], the fledging period is completed approximately 20 days after hatching [tx = approximately 20 days after hatching]. This rapid development to flight-capable independence is characteristic of arctic-breeding shorebirds that must complete their life cycle within a short window of resource abundance. After fledging, juveniles embark on a period of intensive foraging to build the body condition necessary for their first trans-equatorial migration. Sexual maturity, in contrast, is reached considerably later, with puberty typically estimated at 60 days after hatching [tp = 60 days after hatching] under these same thermal conditions at a temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. The attainment of reproductive capability at such a relatively early age—within the same summer season—is notable among small scolopacids. However, most individuals defer actual breeding until the following year, as the energetic demands of migration and gonadal development often preclude successful reproduction in the first year of life.

Life-history data collected from banding studies indicate that the maximum lifespan of the Red-necked phalarope in the wild is approximately 12.9 years [am = approximately 12.9 years] at 41 °C [T = 41 °C], a longevity value derived from the North American Bird Banding Laboratory records. This lifespan is considerable for a bird of its body size and reflects a relatively slow pace of life for a migratory species. Such long-lived individuals represent the upper tail of the distribution, with median survival being substantially lower due to the high mortality risks associated with migration and wintering. The species' longevity is all the more remarkable given that its annual reproductive investment is not negligible. Females lay between 2 and 4 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 2 and 4 eggs per clutch], with a typical frequency of approximately 1.5 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 1.5 clutches per year], producing a maximum annual output that is constrained by the short Arctic summer.

The timing of first reproduction is a critical life-history parameter that reflects the interplay between growth, migration, and breeding opportunity. The time since birth at first brood is estimated at 365 days [tR = 365 days] under the species' active thermal regime of 41 °C [T = 41 °C], meaning that most individuals do not successfully nest until their second calendar year. This delay allows young birds to complete their first full migration cycle and accumulate the somatic reserves necessary for egg production or sustained incubation. The initial wet weight of a chick immediately following yolk absorption and before exogenous feeding, approximately 6.3 grams [Ww0 = approximately 6.3 grams], is slightly higher than the standard hatchling weight at emergence, reflecting the transient yolk contribution that supports the chick during its first hours of independence. Such fine-scale mass measurements are rarely available for wild shorebird populations and underscore the value of detailed captive-rearing studies.
